title: Teach Them to Make Their Own Pacts
hook: A glaze cabinet tag hangs beside two unfinished cup handles. A pact a child owns must be small enough to adjust.
counterintuition: The easy mistake is to make adult rules look like child-made commitments. The sharper move is to guide a child to design a small pact they understand, own, and can adjust after seeing what happens.
tryThisNow: Ask the child to choose one tiny pact for a repeated drift and explain how they will know it worked.
keyTakeaway: Guide a child to design a small pact they understand, own, and can adjust after seeing what happens so prior intent beats the nearest convincing escape.

breakdown.fastRead: A glaze cabinet tag hangs beside two unfinished cup handles. An adult-made rule may stop a child once, but it does not teach ownership. Help the child build a small promise they understand and can revise. Ask what they want, what gets in the way, and what barrier they choose before the pull starts. The pact should feel like their promise, not your trap. Autonomy grows when the child helps design the constraint.
breakdown.deepRead:
Nora points to the glaze cabinet tag while two unfinished cup handles dry on the table. The teen does not need another adult rule about video breaks. The portfolio needs owned studio time, so the pact has to belong to the person who will keep it. Nora asks what risk the teen wants to protect against, then lets the teen choose where the earbuds go until both handles are attached.

Self-authorship is the useful part. A pact handed down from an adult can stop a child once, but it does not teach the child how to design the next constraint. A pact the child helps build has a different feel. It says, I know what pulls me away, and I can place a barrier before the pull starts.

A child-owned pact works when the barrier feels chosen before the screen starts bargaining.

Uma's soccer referee scene gives the same skill a different shape. The whistle stays inside the study box until three offside cards are explained. The point is not to trap the child. The point is to make the child's own plan visible enough to use when the easier option starts to glow.
